data.summary: Leprosy & mycobacterial · 37 viva questions with answers
data.body:
_Viva questions for the case: **Hansen's disease (leprosy)** (Leprosy & mycobacterial)_

**Q1. Define leprosy.**
- Chronic granulomatous infection by Mycobacterium leprae (and M. lepromatosis) that mainly affects skin and peripheral nerves, also eyes, nasal mucosa, testes, bones; clinical spectrum decided by host cell-mediated immunity

**Q2. Describe the organism.**
- Acid-fast (weaker than M. tuberculosis — decolorise with 5% sulphuric acid), Gram-positive, obligate intracellular bacillus; prefers Schwann cells and macrophages
- Generation time ~12–14 days (slowest known); optimum 30–33 °C → cooler parts of body affected (ear lobes, nose, testes, superficial nerves)
- Not cultivable in vitro; grows in mouse foot-pad (Shepard) and nine-banded armadillo
- Cell wall: phenolic glycolipid-1 (PGL-1, species specific — binds laminin-α2 of Schwann cell basal lamina), lipoarabinomannan; genome shows massive gene decay (only ~half functional genes)

**Q3. Transmission and incubation period?**
- Main route: nasal droplets from untreated multibacillary patients → upper respiratory mucosa; less often broken skin; rarely transplacental, insect, armadillo (zoonosis in USA)
- Incubation: average 2–5 years for PB, 8–12 years for MB (range months to decades)
- Most exposed people never develop disease (high natural resistance); household contacts of MB patients have the highest risk

**Q4. What are the cardinal signs of leprosy (NLEP)?**
- 1) Hypopigmented or erythematous skin patch with definite loss of sensation
- 2) Thickened or enlarged peripheral nerve with loss of sensation and/or weakness of muscles supplied by it
- 3) Acid-fast bacilli in slit-skin smear
- Any one sign is enough to diagnose leprosy

**Q5. Give the Ridley–Jopling classification and the immunological basis.**
- TT – BT – BB – BL – LL (+ indeterminate outside the spectrum; pure neuritic separately)
- TT pole: strong Th1 (IFN-γ, IL-2), few bacilli, lepromin positive; LL pole: Th2 (IL-4, IL-10), anergy to M. leprae, plenty of bacilli, lepromin negative
- Borderline groups are immunologically unstable → shift (upgrade/downgrade) and type 1 reactions

**Q6. Give the WHO / NLEP operational classification.**
- Paucibacillary (PB): 1–5 skin lesions, no nerve involvement, smear negative
- Multibacillary (MB): ≥6 skin lesions, OR any nerve involvement (NLEP 2025: any nerve involvement = MB), OR positive slit-skin smear irrespective of lesions
- When in doubt classify as MB

**Q7. Compare TT, BT, BB, BL and LL clinically.**
- TT: 1–3 well-defined dry, scaly, anaesthetic plaques with raised edges, hair loss, one thickened nerve near the lesion
- BT: few–many (≤10) asymmetrical lesions with satellite lesions and irregular edges, sensory loss, several nerves asymmetrically thickened
- BB: many 'punched-out', inverted-saucer or Swiss-cheese lesions with sloping outer edge; unstable
- BL: many lesions, roughly symmetrical, some sensation preserved, many nerves, early nodules
- LL: innumerable symmetrical shiny macules/papules/nodules, diffuse infiltration, leonine facies, madarosis, ear lobe thickening, glove-and-stocking anaesthesia, late nerve damage, systemic involvement

**Q8. What is indeterminate leprosy?**
- Earliest form: one or few vague hypopigmented macules with ill-defined edges and doubtful/slight sensory loss, usually in children; smear negative; nerves not thickened
- Histology: perineural/peri-appendageal lymphocytes, rare bacilli in nerve
- May heal spontaneously or progress to any group

**Q9. What is pure neuritic leprosy?**
- Nerve involvement (thickening, sensory/motor loss) without any skin lesion; ~5–10% in India
- Diagnosis: nerve biopsy (sural or radial cutaneous) or FNAC; treat as MB

**Q10. Which nerves do you palpate and where?**
- Supraorbital, great auricular (neck, across sternomastoid on turning head), ulnar (above medial epicondyle), median (wrist, medial to palmaris longus), radial cutaneous (lateral border of radius at wrist), radial (spiral groove), common peroneal (behind fibular head), superficial peroneal (dorsum of foot), sural, posterior tibial (behind medial malleolus)
- Note: thickening, tenderness, consistency, nodules/abscess; compare both sides

**Q11. Describe the deformities in leprosy and classify them.**
- Primary (due to disease): madarosis, leonine facies, nasal collapse (saddle nose), lagophthalmos, claw hand, foot drop, ape thumb
- Secondary (due to anaesthesia/neglect): ulcers, shortening and absorption of digits, contractures, Charcot joints
- Ulnar claw (ring and little finger), median + ulnar = complete claw with ape-thumb (thenar wasting), radial = wrist drop (rare), common peroneal = foot drop, posterior tibial = claw toes and plantar anaesthesia, facial = lagophthalmos, trigeminal = corneal anaesthesia

**Q12. Grade disability (WHO).**
- Hands and feet: Grade 0 — no anaesthesia, no visible deformity; Grade 1 — anaesthesia, no visible deformity; Grade 2 — visible deformity or damage (ulcers, claw, foot drop, resorption)
- Eyes: Grade 0 normal; Grade 1 — eye problems due to leprosy but vision not severely affected (≥6/60); Grade 2 — lagophthalmos, iridocyclitis, corneal opacity, vision <6/60
- EHF score: sum of grades of 2 eyes, 2 hands, 2 feet (0–12) — better for monitoring

**Q13. How do you do and read a slit-skin smear?**
- Sites: both ear lobes, forehead/eyebrow, active edge of lesions (usually 4–6 sites); blanch skin by pinching, 5 mm long 2–3 mm deep slit, scrape dermal fluid, smear, fix, Ziehl–Neelsen with 5% H2SO4
- Bacteriological index (Ridley log scale, 0 to 6+): 1+ = 1–10 bacilli in 100 fields … 6+ = >1000 per field; average of sites
- Morphological index: % of solid (uniformly stained, viable) bacilli — falls quickly with treatment; BI falls ~0.6–1 log per year

**Q14. What is the Fite–Faraco stain?**
- Modified acid-fast stain using peanut oil–xylene to protect the fragile lipid coat of M. leprae in tissue sections — better than ZN for biopsies

**Q15. Describe the histopathology across the spectrum.**
- TT: well-formed epithelioid granulomas reaching up to epidermis, dense lymphocytic mantle, nerves destroyed, no bacilli
- BT: granulomas with a narrow grenz zone sometimes absent, fewer lymphocytes, nerves swollen, AFB rare
- BB: diffuse epithelioid cells, no giant cells, few lymphocytes, moderate bacilli
- BL: macrophage granulomas with some foamy cells, lymphocytes, 'onion-skin' perineurium
- LL: clear grenz zone (Unna band), sheets of foamy Virchow (lepra) cells with globi, very few lymphocytes, many bacilli

**Q16. What is the lepromin test? How is it read and what is its value?**
- Intradermal injection of 0.1 ml heat-killed M. leprae (Mitsuda/Dharmendra antigen)
- Early Fernandez reaction at 48–72 h (delayed hypersensitivity to soluble antigen); late Mitsuda reaction at 21–28 days (nodule ≥5 mm = positive; reflects ability to mount granulomatous CMI)
- Not diagnostic (positive in healthy people); used for classification and prognosis — negative in LL/BL

**Q17. Other diagnostic tests?**
- Sensory testing: monofilaments (Semmes–Weinstein), ball-pen, temperature/pain tests
- Histamine test (incomplete triple response in anaesthetic patch — sensory nerve loss), sweat test with pilocarpine/starch-iodine (anhidrosis)
- Nerve conduction studies, high-resolution ultrasound of nerves
- Serology: anti-PGL-1 IgM (correlates with bacterial load; useful in MB and contact surveillance)
- PCR for M. leprae DNA (RLEP) — pure neuritic, paucibacillary, relapse; rpoB/folP/gyrA for drug resistance

**Q18. What are lepra reactions? Compare type 1 and type 2.**
- Acute inflammatory episodes during otherwise chronic course, before, during or after MDT; main cause of nerve damage
- Type 1 (reversal reaction): delayed-type hypersensitivity (Th1 up), in borderline cases (BT, BB, BL); existing lesions become red, swollen, tender; new lesions; acute neuritis (pain, tenderness, new loss of function); oedema of hands/feet/face; little systemic upset
- Type 2 (erythema nodosum leprosum, ENL): immune-complex (type III) with neutrophils and high TNF-α, in BL/LL with high BI; crops of tender evanescent red nodules on normal skin, fever, malaise, neuritis, iridocyclitis, orchitis, arthritis, lymphadenitis, nephritis, dactylitis; often recurrent/chronic

**Q19. How do you treat type 1 reaction?**
- Continue MDT; rest, splint affected nerves, analgesics
- Prednisolone 40 mg/day (≈1 mg/kg) tapering slowly: e.g. 40 mg ×2 wk, 30, 25, 20, 15, 10, 5 mg in 2–4 weekly steps — about 12 weeks for PB and 20–24 weeks for MB/neuritis
- Severe neuritis not responding: higher dose, then consider nerve decompression

**Q20. How do you treat ENL?**
- Mild: NSAIDs, rest
- Moderate–severe: prednisolone 40–60 mg/day with taper (short course)
- Chronic/recurrent: clofazimine 100 mg three times daily up to 12 weeks then taper (total ≤12 months) — steroid-sparing, slow onset
- Thalidomide 100–400 mg/day (very effective; teratogenic — not in women of child-bearing age without strict contraception; neuropathy, thrombosis); pentoxifylline, methotrexate, minocycline also used

**Q21. What is the Lucio phenomenon?**
- Occurs in untreated diffuse non-nodular lepromatous leprosy (Lucio–Latapi, 'lepra bonita' with smooth shiny skin) — Mexico/Central America
- Necrotising vasculitis by bacilli in endothelium → painful purpuric angular lesions becoming haemorrhagic bullae and ulcers on limbs, without fever
- Treat with MDT + steroids, wound care; may need exchange transfusion in severe cases

**Q22. What is histoid leprosy?**
- Variant of LL (often after dapsone monotherapy or irregular treatment) with soft, shiny skin-coloured to red papules and nodules on apparently normal skin, especially over joints and back
- Histology: spindle-shaped histiocytes in a whorled/storiform pattern with huge numbers of bacilli (high BI) — a source of drug resistance and transmission

**Q23. Name the other clinical variants.**
- Lazarine leprosy (ulcerating lesions in borderline cases without neuritis)
- Lepra bonita / Lucio leprosy, histoid, pure neuritic, conjugal leprosy (between spouses, low rate)
- Childhood leprosy (indicator of active transmission in the community)
- Leprosy in HIV (more type 1 reactions after ART — immune reconstitution)

**Q24. What is the MDT regimen now (NLEP from 1 April 2025)?**
- Same 3 drugs for both PB and MB: rifampicin + clofazimine + dapsone; PB for 6 months, MB for 12 months
- Adult (>14 y): monthly supervised rifampicin 600 mg + clofazimine 300 mg; daily self-administered clofazimine 50 mg + dapsone 100 mg
- Child 10–14 y: rifampicin 450 mg + clofazimine 150 mg monthly; clofazimine 50 mg alternate days + dapsone 50 mg daily
- Child <10 y: by weight — rifampicin 10 mg/kg monthly, clofazimine 6 mg/kg monthly + 1 mg/kg alternate days, dapsone 2 mg/kg daily
- Blister packs: adult (red for MB), child (yellow); release from treatment after completing the course (PB in 6 within 9 months, MB in 12 within 18 months)

**Q25. Mechanism of action and important side effects of MDT drugs.**
- Rifampicin: inhibits DNA-dependent RNA polymerase (rpoB) — kills 99.9% with one dose; red urine, hepatitis, flu-like syndrome/thrombocytopenia with intermittent dosing, enzyme inducer (reduces OCP and steroid efficacy)
- Dapsone: blocks folate synthesis (dihydropteroate synthase; folP); haemolysis (worse in G6PD deficiency), methaemoglobinaemia, agranulocytosis, dapsone hypersensitivity syndrome (~4–6 weeks; fever, rash, hepatitis, lymphadenopathy; HLA-B*13:01), neuropathy
- Clofazimine: binds mycobacterial DNA, anti-inflammatory; reddish-brown pigmentation and ichthyosis (reversible slowly), GI crystal deposition (abdominal pain), dry skin

**Q26. Newer drugs / alternative regimens?**
- Ofloxacin/levofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin — for drug intolerance or resistance
- Rifampicin resistance: 24 months of daily clofazimine with two of ofloxacin/moxifloxacin, minocycline, clarithromycin (WHO)
- Rifapentine, bedaquiline under study

**Q27. What is chemoprophylaxis of leprosy?**
- Single-dose rifampicin (SDR-PEP) to contacts of new cases after excluding leprosy and TB — adults 600 mg; children by age/weight (not under 2 years)
- Reduces risk in contacts by about 50–60% in the first 2 years (COLEP)
- Used under NLEP in contact tracing campaigns (LCDC)

**Q28. Vaccines in leprosy?**
- BCG gives variable protection (≈ 26–50%); repeat BCG adds some
- Mycobacterium indicus pranii (MIP, formerly Mw) — immunotherapy with MDT and in contacts (Indian vaccine)
- LepVax (LEP-F1) in trials

**Q29. Define relapse; differentiate it from type 1 reaction.**
- Relapse: re-appearance of disease activity after successful completion of MDT (new lesions, new nerve damage, rise in BI ≥2+ at any site)
- Reaction: sudden onset (days), within ~6 months of stopping MDT, existing lesions inflamed, often tender nerves, rapid response to steroids (2–4 weeks), BI not rising
- Relapse: insidious onset, usually >3 years after RFT, new lesions slowly, no response to steroid trial, BI rises/solid bacilli

**Q30. What are persisters and resisters?**
- Persisters: drug-sensitive but dormant viable bacilli that survive despite therapy (in nerves, smooth muscle, bone marrow) — cause late relapse
- Resisters: genetically drug-resistant bacilli (mutations in rpoB, folP1, gyrA) — primary or secondary (after monotherapy)

**Q31. How is the eye involved?**
- Lagophthalmos (facial nerve, zygomatic branch — in reactions), corneal anaesthesia (trigeminal) → exposure keratitis and ulcer
- Madarosis, iridocyclitis (acute in ENL, chronic in LL), scleritis, iris pearls, cataract, secondary glaucoma
- Vision loss → grade 2 disability; needs eye exercises, goggles, tarsorrhaphy if severe

**Q32. Systemic involvement in lepromatous leprosy?**
- Nose: stuffiness, epistaxis, septal perforation, saddle nose
- Testes: atrophy → infertility, gynaecomastia
- Bones: absorption of phalanges, maxilla (facies leprosa); osteoporosis
- Kidney: amyloidosis, glomerulonephritis (ENL); liver, lymph nodes, larynx (hoarseness)

**Q33. What is the role of reconstructive surgery? (short note)**
- Only after disease and reactions are inactive for ≥6 months
- Tendon transfers: claw hand — Brand's procedures/lasso; foot drop — tibialis posterior transfer; ape thumb — opponensplasty
- Eyebrow reconstruction (hair grafts), nasal reconstruction, tarsorrhaphy for lagophthalmos; nerve decompression for abscess/neuritis

**Q34. Prevention of disability and care of anaesthetic hands/feet?**
- Soak, scrape (oil), oil daily for dry skin; inspect for cracks and wounds; protective footwear (MCR micro-cellular rubber chappals), avoid hot objects
- Self-care groups; splints and physiotherapy for weak muscles; early steroid for neuritis
- Ulcer: rest, cleaning, dressing, offloading; avoid walking on ulcerated foot

**Q35. Differential diagnosis of hypopigmented patches (common short note).**
- Pityriasis alba, pityriasis versicolor, nevus depigmentosus/anaemicus, post-inflammatory hypopigmentation, vitiligo (depigmented), indeterminate leprosy, hypopigmented mycosis fungoides, idiopathic guttate hypomelanosis, progressive macular hypomelanosis, sarcoidosis, PKDL (post-kala-azar)
- Sensation, nerve thickening and smear help separate leprosy

**Q36. Differential diagnosis of nodular lesions as in LL.**
- PKDL (no sensory loss, LD bodies), neurofibromatosis, cutaneous leishmaniasis, sarcoidosis, lymphoma/leukaemia cutis, xanthomas, secondary syphilis, multiple histiocytomas, Kaposi sarcoma, onchocerciasis

**Q37. Leprosy elimination status in India?**
- Elimination as a public health problem (prevalence <1/10,000) achieved nationally in December 2005; some districts still above
- National Strategic Plan aims at interruption of transmission / zero new cases by 2027 (SDG target 2030)
- Indicators: new case detection rate, grade 2 disability per million, child proportion

## Quick spotter facts
- Cardinal signs — anaesthetic patch, thick nerve, positive smear (any one)
- Lucio phenomenon — diffuse LL + necrotic angular ulcers without fever
- Histoid — shiny nodules, spindle cells, very high BI

## Note
Doses and duration follow the NLEP revised regimen (effective 1 April 2025) as already used in Exam drugs; check with the department for local practice.

_Sources: Previous-year PG question papers (Sahana P Raju, Solved Papers Dermatology); IADVL Textbook of Dermatology 5e (leprosy chapters); NLEP revised MDT guidance effective 1 April 2025; WHO disability grading. Answers written in our own words; check with your teachers' preferences._
